college.stem: After an injury to part of the prefrontal cortex, a man reports that very little stirs him emotionally, and his everyday choices become noticeably worse. What does this case suggest about emotion and decision making?
options: Emotion appears to support sound decisions, since weakened emotion accompanies poorer choices.
Emotion appears to interfere with decisions, so weakened emotion should produce better choices.
Prefrontal damage harms choices only in people who were very optimistic beforehand.
Weakened emotion alters memory for earlier choices but leaves new choices untouched.
college.why: People with damage to an area of the prefrontal cortex who suffer from flattened emotions have impaired decision making, so emotion contributes to good choices. The idea that removing emotion improves choices runs opposite to that finding.

simple.stem: People with damage to part of the prefrontal cortex can have flattened emotions. How does this affect their decisions?
options: Their ability to make good decisions is impaired.
Their decisions become more accurate and careful.
Their decisions stay exactly the same as before.
They lose the ability to make any choice.
simple.why: Flattened emotions after prefrontal damage go with impaired decision making. Losing emotion does not make decisions better or leave them unchanged.

college.stem: A nervous homeowner turns down every investment that carries any chance of a large loss, even when success is likely. Which pattern, typical of anxious people, does this describe?
options: Risk avoidance, steering away from choices that could bring large negative consequences.
Status quo bias, sticking with whatever option happens to be the default.
Belief bias, accepting a conclusion mainly because it sounds believable.
Excessive optimism, ignoring negative information and attending only to positive information.
college.why: Anxious people tend to avoid decisions that could lead to large negative consequences, which is risk avoidance. Excessive optimism is the opposite pattern, in which negative information is ignored.

simple.stem: Anxious people tend to avoid choices that could lead to big negative outcomes. What is this called?
options: This pattern is called risk avoidance.
This pattern is called the framing effect.
This pattern is called belief bias.
This pattern is called the status quo bias.
simple.why: Avoiding decisions that could bring large negative consequences is risk avoidance. The framing effect, belief bias and the status quo bias describe other tendencies.

college.stem: Before agreeing to a wager, a woman pictures how disappointed she will be if she loses. Which term best fits the feeling she is anticipating?
options: An expected emotion, one a person predicts feeling about an outcome.
An incidental emotion, one unrelated to the decision and arising from surroundings.
A permission schema, a familiar rule linking a condition to an allowed action.
A flattened emotion, one dulled by damage to the prefrontal cortex.
college.why: Expected emotions are emotions people predict they will feel concerning an outcome, and they help determine risk aversion. An incidental emotion is unrelated to the decision itself.

simple.stem: What are expected emotions?
options: Emotions people predict they will feel about an outcome.
Emotions caused by the weather or surroundings that day.
Emotions people felt in the past about a similar choice.
Emotions that other people show while making a decision.
simple.why: Expected emotions are the feelings people predict they will have about an outcome. Feelings caused by the weather or surroundings are incidental emotions.

college.stem: A man declines a coin-flip bet to win or lose $20 because he is sure that losing would feel far worse than winning would feel good. Which principle explains the refusal?
options: Believing a loss will weigh more than an equal gain increases risk aversion.
Believing a gain will weigh more than an equal loss increases risk aversion.
Expected emotions influence risk taking but play no part in avoiding risk.
People forecast their feelings accurately, so his choice mirrors his true reactions.
college.why: The belief that a loss will have a greater impact than a gain of the same size increases risk aversion. People also predict their emotions inaccurately, so the forecast need not match his real reaction.

simple.stem: Some people believe a loss will affect them more than a gain of the same size. What does this belief do?
options: It makes them more likely to avoid taking risks.
It makes them more likely to seek out risks.
It makes them predict their feelings perfectly.
It has no effect on the risks they take.
simple.why: Believing a loss will hurt more than an equal gain helps increases risk aversion. It does not make people seek risk, and people predict their feelings inaccurately.

college.stem: A researcher wants to test whether people misjudge how they will feel about outcomes. Which comparison would test this most directly?
options: Compare the feelings people forecast for an outcome with those they report once it occurs.
Compare how often people pick a sure option when outcomes are worded as gains versus losses.
Compare organ-donor consent rates in countries using opt-in versus opt-out procedures.
Compare how often people turn over the E card versus the 4 card in the four-card problem.
college.why: Showing that predictions are inaccurate requires placing predicted feelings beside actual feelings, the comparison Kermer and colleagues (2006) made. The other comparisons concern framing, defaults and conditional reasoning.

simple.stem: How could a researcher check whether people predict their own feelings accurately?
options: Compare predicted feelings with the feelings people report later.
Ask people only how they feel before anything happens.
Ask people only how they feel after the outcome happens.
Compare how the same people feel on sunny days and on cloudy days.
simple.why: Accuracy can be judged only by comparing the predicted feeling with the actual feeling. Asking at just one time point gives nothing to compare.

college.stem: In Kermer and colleagues’ (2006) study, participants received $5 and were told a coin flip would decide what happened next. What were the two possible results of the flip?
options: They would win an additional $5 or else lose $3.
They would win an additional $3 or else lose $5.
They would double their $5 or else lose all of it.
They would keep their $5 or else hand it to someone else.
college.why: Participants were given $5 and told that a coin flip would decide whether they won another $5 or lost $3. The amounts were not reversed, and no outcome involved losing everything.

simple.stem: In Kermer and colleagues’ (2006) coin-flip study, what could participants win or lose?
options: They could win $5 more or lose $3.
They could win $3 more or lose $5.
They could win $10 more or lose $10.
They could win a prize or lose nothing.
simple.why: After receiving $5, participants learned they would either win an additional $5 or lose $3 on a coin flip.

college.stem: When Kermer and colleagues (2006) compared predicted and actual happiness after losing the coin flip, what did they find?
options: Participants overestimated their negative feeling, because the loss hurt far less than they had forecast.
Participants underestimated their negative feeling, because the loss hurt far more than they had forecast.
Predicted and actual unhappiness after the loss turned out to be the same size.
Losing raised happiness above baseline, whereas winning lowered it below baseline.
college.why: Before the flip, people expected losing to lower their happiness by roughly 4 points, but the actual drop was only about 1 point. They overestimated their negative feeling rather than underestimating it.

simple.stem: What did Kermer and colleagues (2006) find about how people expected to feel after losing?
options: People expected to feel worse than they really did.
People expected to feel better than they really did.
People predicted their feelings exactly right.
People felt happier after losing than after winning.
simple.why: People overestimated their negative feeling: losing hurt much less than they predicted.

college.stem: In Kermer and colleagues’ (2006) coin-flip study, why were participants’ forecasts of their feelings after losing so far off?
options: Coping mechanisms kick in after a loss, but people ignore them when predicting emotions.
Participants forgot how much money was at stake before making their forecasts.
The happiness scale gave participants no way at all to report negative feelings about losing.
Participants had been told they would win, so the loss came as a shock.
college.why: We usually have coping mechanisms that get activated after a loss, but we do not take them into account when predicting emotions. Those mechanisms soften the actual feeling.

simple.stem: In Kermer and colleagues’ (2006) study, why did people overestimate how bad losing would feel?
options: They did not consider that coping would soften the feeling.
They forgot how much money they could lose.
They were told ahead of time that they would surely win the bet.
They were unable to feel any negative emotions.
simple.why: Coping mechanisms get activated after a loss, but people do not consider them when predicting how they will feel.

college.stem: In Kermer and colleagues’ (2006) study, participants expected losing $3 to lower their happiness about twice as much as winning $5 would raise it. Why is this result striking?
options: The loss was the smaller sum of money, yet it was expected to matter more than the larger gain.
The gain was the smaller sum of money, so a smaller expected rise fits the amounts exactly.
The two sums were equal, so any gap in expected feeling must be random error.
The forecasts were collected after the flip, so they reflect actual rather than predicted feelings.
college.why: Losing $3 is less money than winning $5, yet people expected the loss to change their happiness about twice as much. This fits the belief that losses have a greater impact than gains.

simple.stem: In Kermer and colleagues’ (2006) study, which outcome did people expect to affect their happiness more?
options: Losing $3, even though it was less money than the $5 gain.
Winning $5, because it was the larger amount of money.
Both outcomes were expected to matter exactly the same.
Neither outcome was expected to change their happiness.
simple.why: People expected losing $3 to lower happiness about twice as much as winning $5 would raise it, even though the loss was the smaller amount.

college.stem: After a frustrating commute, a manager makes a hasty hiring decision later that morning. What kind of emotion may be shaping the choice?
options: An incidental emotion, one unrelated to the decision and arising from a recent experience.
An expected emotion, one the manager forecasts feeling about how the new hire eventually turns out.
A permission schema, a familiar rule stating when an action may be carried out.
A mental model, an imagined situation used to check whether a conclusion is valid.
college.why: Incidental emotions are not specifically related to the decision and may come from disposition, a recent experience or the surroundings. An expected emotion would concern the outcome of the hire itself.

simple.stem: What are incidental emotions?
options: Emotions not specifically related to the decision being made.
Emotions that people predict they will feel about an outcome later.
Emotions that come only from the decision itself.
Emotions that appear only after damage to the brain.
simple.why: Incidental emotions are not specifically related to the decision; they can come from personality, a recent experience or the surroundings. Predicted feelings about an outcome are expected emotions.

college.stem: Simonsohn (2007) analyzed university admissions decisions made under different weather conditions. What pattern emerged?
options: Applicants’ academic attributes received more weight on cloudy days than on sunny days.
Applicants’ academic attributes received more weight on sunny days than on cloudy days.
The weather on the day of review had no detectable effect on the decisions.
Applicants who toured the campus on cloudy days were less likely to be admitted.
college.why: Simonsohn (2007) found academic attributes were weighted more heavily on cloudy days, so an incidental factor shifted what decision makers emphasized. The cloudy-day campus visit finding is a separate study about enrollment, Simonsohn (2009).

simple.stem: What did Simonsohn (2007) find about university admissions decisions and the weather?
options: Academic qualities counted more on cloudy days.
Academic qualities counted more on sunny days.
The weather made no difference to admissions decisions.
Admissions officers rejected more applicants on rainy days.
simple.why: Applicants’ academic attributes were weighted more heavily on cloudy days than on sunny days, showing an incidental influence on decisions.

college.stem: In Lerner and colleagues’ (2004) study, participants watched one of three film clips before pricing highlighters. Which clip was used to induce disgust?
options: A clip showing a person using a dirty toilet.
A clip showing a person who was dying.
A clip showing fish at the Great Barrier Reef.
A clip showing a person selling a box of highlighters.
college.why: The disgust clip showed a person using a dirty toilet. The clip of a person dying created sadness, and the Great Barrier Reef clip was neutral.

simple.stem: In Lerner and colleagues’ (2004) study, which film clip was meant to make people feel disgusted?
options: A person using a dirty toilet.
A person who was dying.
Fish swimming at the Great Barrier Reef.
A person shopping for highlighters.
simple.why: The dirty-toilet clip was the disgust condition; the dying person was the sad condition and the reef was neutral.

college.stem: Relative to the neutral group in Lerner and colleagues’ (2004) study, how did sad participants price the highlighters?
options: They set a lower selling price and offered a higher buying price.
They set a higher selling price and offered a lower buying price.
They set lower prices for both selling and buying the highlighters.
They set selling and buying prices equal to those of the neutral group.
college.why: Sad participants asked about $3.00 to sell, below the neutral group’s roughly $4.50, and offered about $4.50 to buy, above the neutral roughly $3.50. Lowering both prices fits the disgust group more closely than the sad group.

simple.stem: In Lerner and colleagues’ (2004) study, how did sadness change what people would pay to buy the highlighters?
options: Sad people offered more to buy than neutral people.
Sad people offered less to buy than neutral people.
Sad people offered the same as neutral people.
Sad people refused to buy the highlighters at all.
simple.why: Sad participants offered about $4.50 to buy, compared with about $3.50 in the neutral group.

college.stem: Why do the highlighter prices in Lerner and colleagues’ (2004) study count as evidence about incidental emotions?
options: The clips were unrelated to highlighters, so price shifts reflect mood unrelated to the decision.
The clips were all about highlighters, so price shifts reflect expected feelings about owning one.
Every group watched the same clip, so price shifts must come from personality alone.
Participants picked their own clip, so each mood matched the price they already preferred.
college.why: Each clip created a mood unrelated to the highlighters, so a change in price shows that a person’s mood can influence decision making. The clips were not about highlighters, and the groups saw different clips.

simple.stem: What did Lerner and colleagues’ (2004) film-clip study show about decisions?
options: A person’s mood can influence their decisions.
Prices depend only on the real value of the item.
Mood affects decisions only when it concerns the item.
Film clips make people refuse to buy anything.
simple.why: Unrelated clips changed the prices people set, which shows that a person’s mood can influence decision making.

college.stem: Physicians judged the same hypothetical cesarean candidate under three conditions. After which preceding cases did significantly more of them recommend a cesarean?
options: After first reviewing four fairly routine cases without serious complications.
After first reviewing four cases that each involved serious medical complications.
When the test case came first, with no cases before it.
After reviewing the same test case twice in a row.
college.why: Significantly more doctors recommended a cesarean after first reviewing non-serious cases. The test case itself never changed, so the preceding cases changed the decision.

simple.stem: Doctors judged a possible cesarean case after looking at other cases. When did more doctors recommend a cesarean?
options: When the earlier cases were routine and not serious.
When the earlier cases had serious complications.
When the test case came with no earlier cases.
When the doctors saw the test case two times.
simple.why: More doctors recommended a cesarean when the test case followed four fairly routine cases.

college.stem: Why does the cesarean study with physicians support the claim that decisions depend on the context in which they are made?
options: The test case stayed identical across conditions, and only the cases reviewed before it differed.
The test case differed across conditions, while the cases reviewed before it stayed the same.
Physicians in each condition were told which recommendation the researchers expected.
Each physician judged a different patient, so differences reflect the patients themselves.
college.why: Holding the test case constant and varying only the preceding cases isolates the effect of context on the recommendation. If the test case itself had changed, context could not be singled out.

simple.stem: In the cesarean study with physicians, what stayed the same across all three conditions?
options: The test case that the doctors had to judge.
The cases that the doctors reviewed beforehand.
The number of serious cases the doctors saw first.
The recommendation that every doctor gave.
simple.why: The test case was the same in every condition; only the cases before it changed, and the recommendations differed.

college.stem: A country changes its organ-donation system from requiring people to sign up to counting everyone as a donor unless they ask not to be. What shift in consent would be expected?
options: Consent would rise sharply, since people tend to stay with the default and do nothing.
Consent would drop sharply, since people resist a default that has been imposed.
Consent would stay unchanged, since donation choices rest only on their benefits.
Consent would rise only among people who already felt anxious about donating.
college.why: Opt-in countries have consent rates below 28%, whereas opt-out countries have rates above 99%. The status quo bias, doing nothing when facing a difficult decision, keeps people in whichever option is the default.

simple.stem: Which organ-donation system leads to more people becoming donors?
options: Opt-out, where people are donors unless they ask not to be.
Opt-in, where people must take an active step to sign up as donors.
Both systems lead to the same number of donors.
Neither system has any effect on how many donate.
simple.why: Opt-out countries have far higher consent rates than opt-in countries, because people tend to do nothing and keep the default.

college.stem: Faced with a hard choice among retirement plans, an employee simply leaves her savings in the plan she was automatically enrolled in. Which tendency does this illustrate?
options: The status quo bias, the tendency to do nothing when facing a difficult decision.
The framing effect, the tendency to choose differently depending on how options are worded.
Belief bias, the tendency to accept conclusions that sound believable.
Risk taking under a loss frame, the tendency to favor a gamble.
college.why: The status quo bias is the tendency to do nothing when faced with a difficult decision, so the default plan stays in place. Nothing about the wording of the plans or a gamble is involved.

simple.stem: What is the status quo bias?
options: The tendency to do nothing when a decision is difficult.
The tendency to always choose the newest option.
The tendency to take risks when facing losses.
The tendency to trust conclusions that sound believable.
simple.why: The status quo bias is the tendency to do nothing when faced with a difficult decision. Trusting believable conclusions is belief bias.

college.stem: In the short story “The International Community,” a king’s chef asks the summoned birds which sauce they would like to be eaten with, and dismisses a bird that does not want to be eaten at all. What point about decisions does the story illustrate?
options: The options offered can limit a choice, since not being eaten was never among them.
The birds could decline to be eaten simply by asking the chef politely.
The chef let the birds choose between being eaten and being set free.
The birds picked their preferred sauce long before they were ever summoned to the summit.
college.why: The chef rules out not being eaten, so the only choice offered is the sauce. Decisions depend on how choices are set up, and here the most important option was never on the table.

simple.stem: In the story about the chef and the birds, what choice were the birds really given?
options: They could choose only the sauce they would be eaten with.
They could choose whether or not to be eaten.
They could choose to leave the summit and fly safely back home.
They could choose which bird would be eaten first.
simple.why: The chef offered a choice of sauce only and refused the option of not being eaten, showing how the way choices are set up shapes a decision.

college.stem: One patient hears that a surgery has a 90% survival rate, another hears that it has a 10% death rate, and the two decide differently. What phenomenon does this illustrate?
options: The framing effect, in which decisions depend on how a choice is stated.
The status quo bias, in which people do nothing when a choice is difficult.
Belief bias, in which believable conclusions are judged to be valid.
An incidental emotion, in which an unrelated mood shapes a choice.
college.why: The framing effect is that decisions are influenced by how a decision is stated, which can highlight one aspect such as survival or death. The two statements describe the same odds.

simple.stem: What is the framing effect?
options: Decisions are influenced by how a choice is worded.
Decisions depend only on the odds of each outcome.
Decisions are influenced by the weather that day.
Decisions depend on how many premises an argument has.
simple.why: The framing effect means decisions are influenced by how a decision is stated, not only by the odds.

college.stem: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) studied how framing alters risky choices. When a situation is framed in terms of losses, which strategy do people tend to adopt?
options: They lean toward a risk-taking strategy and favor the gamble.
They lean toward a risk-averse strategy and favor the sure thing.
They do nothing at all because of the status quo bias.
They reject every option that is placed in front of them.
college.why: With a loss frame people tend toward risk taking, and with a gain frame they tend toward risk aversion. Favoring the sure thing is the gain-frame pattern.

simple.stem: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) studied framing. When choices are framed as losses, what do people tend to do?
options: They tend to take more risks.
They tend to avoid risks more.
They tend to make no choice at all.
They tend to pick options at random.
simple.why: Loss frames push people toward risk taking; gain frames push them toward risk aversion.

college.stem: A disease is expected to kill 600 people. When the two programs to combat it were described in terms of lives saved, which did most people choose?
options: Program A, which saves 200 people for certain, chosen by 72%.
Program B, the 1/3 chance of saving all 600, chosen by 72%.
Program A, which saves 200 people for certain, chosen by 28%.
Program B, the gamble that might save everyone, chosen by 78%.
college.why: With outcomes stated as lives saved, 72% chose the sure Program A and 28% chose the gamble, Program B. This is the risk-averse pattern expected under a gain frame.

simple.stem: A disease is expected to kill 600 people. When the choices were worded as lives saved, what did most people pick?
options: The sure option of saving 200 people.
The gamble with a 1/3 chance of saving everyone.
Neither program, because both seemed too risky.
Both programs, each picked by about half.
simple.why: 72% chose Program A, the sure saving of 200 people, over the gamble.

college.stem: A disease is expected to kill 600 people. When the two programs were described in terms of deaths, which did most people choose?
options: Program D, the gamble with a 1/3 chance that no one dies, chosen by 78%.
Program C, under which 400 people die for certain, chosen by 78%.
Program D, the gamble with a 1/3 chance that no one dies, chosen by 22%.
Program C, under which 200 people are saved, chosen by 72%.
college.why: With outcomes stated as deaths, 78% chose the gamble, Program D, and only 22% chose the sure Program C. This is the risk-taking pattern expected under a loss frame.

simple.stem: A disease is expected to kill 600 people. When the choices were worded in terms of deaths, what did most people pick?
options: The gamble with a 1/3 chance that no one dies.
The sure option in which 400 people die.
Neither program, since both involved deaths.
Both programs, each picked by about half.
simple.why: 78% chose Program D, the gamble, over the sure loss of 400 lives.

college.stem: Program A saves 200 of 600 people for certain; Program C means 400 of 600 people die for certain. Why does the drop from 72% choosing A to 22% choosing C demonstrate framing?
options: A and C produce the same outcome, so only the wording differed between versions.
A saves more people than C, so the drop reflects the better outcome of A.
C has higher odds of success than A, so the drop is a rational shift.
A and C concern different diseases, so the two choices cannot be compared.
college.why: Saving 200 of 600 means 400 die, so A and C are the same outcome. The majority choice changed only because the outcome was stated as saving rather than dying.

simple.stem: Program A says 200 of 600 people will be saved. Program C says 400 of 600 people will die. How do these two programs compare?
options: They describe the same result in different words.
Program A saves more people than Program C.
Program C saves more people than Program A.
Program C involves a gamble, while Program A does not.
simple.why: If 200 of 600 are saved, 400 die, so the programs are identical; only the wording differs, which is why the shift in choices shows framing.

college.stem: Neuroeconomics brings together research from which three fields?
options: Research from psychology, neuroscience, and economics combined.
Research from psychology, linguistics, and philosophy combined.
Research from neuroscience, logic, and computer science combined.
Research from economics, sociology, and anthropology combined.
college.why: Neuroeconomics combines research from psychology, neuroscience, and economics. The other lists each leave out at least one of those fields.

simple.stem: What fields does neuroeconomics combine?
options: Psychology, neuroscience, and economics
Psychology, linguistics, and philosophy
Neuroscience, logic, and computer science
Economics, sociology, and anthropology
simple.why: Neuroeconomics combines psychology, neuroscience, and economics.

college.stem: A team scans participants’ brains while they decide whether to accept offers of money. Which neuroeconomics finding would guide their predictions?
options: Decisions are swayed by emotions, which are linked to activity in specific brain areas.
Money decisions are purely rational calculations and are unrelated to emotional brain activity.
Brain activity during choices tracks only the size of the sum offered.
Emotion sways decisions only when people are told how a choice is framed.
college.why: One finding of neuroeconomics is that decisions are influenced by emotions, and those emotions are associated with activity in specific brain areas. Treating money decisions as purely rational ignores that finding.

simple.stem: What is one finding of neuroeconomics?
options: Emotions influence decisions and are tied to certain brain areas.
Decisions are made without any influence at all from a person’s emotions.
Only the amount of money matters in a decision.
Brain activity has no connection to decision making.
simple.why: Neuroeconomics finds that emotions influence decisions and that those emotions are tied to activity in specific brain areas.

college.stem: In the ultimatum game used by Sanfey and colleagues (2003), a proposer receives $10 and offers the responder a split. What happens if the responder rejects the offer?
options: Neither player receives any of the money.
The proposer keeps the entire $10 alone.
The responder receives the entire $10 instead.
The money is divided evenly between both players.
college.why: The responder can accept or reject the proposed split, and if the responder rejects it, neither player receives anything. The proposer does not keep the money.

simple.stem: In the ultimatum game used by Sanfey and colleagues (2003), what happens when the responder says no to the offer?
options: Both players walk away with nothing.
The proposer keeps all of the money.
The responder gets all of the money.
The two players split the money evenly.
simple.why: A rejection means neither player receives anything.

college.stem: Why does the rule that a rejection leaves both players with nothing make the ultimatum game, as used by Sanfey and colleagues (2003), useful for studying emotion?
options: A rejection gives up real money, so it signals that something other than money is at work.
Rejecting earns the responder extra money, so rejections reveal simple greed.
The proposer must accept any counteroffer the responder makes, so both players always come out ahead.
The total sum changes every round, so responders cannot compare the offers.
college.why: Because a rejection costs both players, choosing to reject means giving up money. That makes it possible to see when something like anger, rather than the money, drives the decision.

simple.stem: In the ultimatum game used by Sanfey and colleagues (2003), why is it surprising when a responder rejects a low offer?
options: Rejecting means giving up money they could have kept.
Rejecting gives the responder even more money.
Rejecting forces the proposer to pay double.
Rejecting is not allowed under the official rules of the game.
simple.why: A rejection leaves both players with nothing, so the responder gives up money; choosing that anyway points to emotion such as anger.

college.stem: In Sanfey and colleagues’ (2003) study, how did participants treat low offers from computer partners compared with the same offers from human partners?
options: They accepted low computer offers more often, being less angry with an unfair computer.
They rejected low computer offers more often, because they distrusted the machines.
They treated low offers the same way no matter who the partner was.
They never received low offers from computers, so no comparison existed.
college.why: An $8 and $2 split was accepted roughly 53% of the time from a human but about 85% of the time from a computer. Participants were less angry with an unfair computer.

simple.stem: In Sanfey and colleagues’ (2003) study, why were unfair offers from a computer accepted more often?
options: People were less angry with an unfair computer.
Computer offers always involved more money.
People could not tell the offers were unfair.
Computers punished people who rejected offers.
simple.why: Low offers were often rejected out of anger at unfairness, and people were less angry when a computer made the unfair offer.

college.stem: In Sanfey and colleagues’ (2003) study, which brain result accompanied rejecting more offers?
options: Greater activation of the right anterior insula, an area tied to emotional states.
Reduced activation of the right anterior insula, an area tied to language.
Greater activation of the hippocampus, an area tied to memory for numbers and amounts.
Damage to the prefrontal cortex, which flattens emotional responses.
college.why: Participants with more activation of the right anterior insula, which is connected with emotional states, were more likely to reject more offers. The direction was greater, not reduced, activation.

simple.stem: In Sanfey and colleagues’ (2003) study, more activity in which brain area went with rejecting more offers?
options: The right anterior insula, linked to emotion.
The hippocampus, which is linked to memory.
The cerebellum, which helps control movement.
The visual cortex, which processes what we see.
simple.why: More activation of the right anterior insula, an area connected with emotional states, went with rejecting more offers.

college.stem: Which description best captures deductive reasoning?
options: Determining whether a conclusion follows logically from a set of premises.
Drawing likely conclusions from many repeated observations of events.
Choosing among alternatives based on the emotions one expects to feel.
Judging how likely an event is by how easily instances come to mind.
college.why: Deductive reasoning is determining whether a conclusion logically follows from premises, and the syllogism is its basic form. Drawing likely conclusions from observations is a different kind of reasoning.

simple.stem: What is deductive reasoning?
options: Deciding if a conclusion logically follows from premises.
Guessing what is likely to happen based on your past experience.
Choosing based on how you expect to feel.
Deciding how a choice should be worded.
simple.why: Deductive reasoning means determining whether a conclusion logically follows from the premises.

college.stem: Premise 1: All birds are animals. Premise 2: All animals have four legs. Conclusion: All birds have four legs. How should this syllogism be judged?
options: Valid, because the conclusion follows from the premises even though it is false.
Invalid, because a syllogism with a false conclusion cannot be valid.
Valid and true, because it shares its form with a true syllogism.
Invalid, because categorical syllogisms are not allowed to describe physical features of animals.
college.why: Validity concerns whether the conclusion follows from the premises, and this syllogism has the same form as the valid syllogism concluding that all birds eat food. Its second premise is false, so its conclusion is false despite being valid.

simple.stem: All birds are animals. All animals have four legs. So, all birds have four legs. Is this syllogism valid?
options: Yes, because the conclusion follows from the premises.
No, because birds do not have four legs.
No, because the second premise is false.
Yes, because every single statement in it is completely true.
simple.why: It is valid because the conclusion follows logically from the premises. A false premise makes the conclusion false, but it does not make the reasoning invalid.

college.stem: A friend claims that a valid syllogism always has a true conclusion. What correction should be made?
options: A valid syllogism must have a true conclusion only when its premises are true.
A valid syllogism has a true conclusion no matter what its premises say.
A valid syllogism never has a true conclusion, because validity concerns form only.
A valid syllogism has a true conclusion only when it uses the word some.
college.why: If the two premises of a valid syllogism are true, its conclusion must be true. A valid form with a false premise can still produce a false conclusion.

simple.stem: A syllogism is valid and both of its premises are true. What must be true of its conclusion?
options: The conclusion must also be true.
The conclusion must turn out false.
The conclusion could be either true or false.
The conclusion must be believable but may be false.
simple.why: When a syllogism is valid and its premises are true, the conclusion must be true.

college.stem: Premise 1: All of the students are tired. Premise 2: Some tired people are irritable. Conclusion: Some of the students are irritable. What does this syllogism illustrate?
options: Each statement sounds reasonable, yet the syllogism is not valid.
Each statement is false, yet the syllogism is still valid.
The syllogism is valid because its conclusion is believable.
The syllogism is invalid simply because it contains the word some.
college.why: Syllogisms can be invalid even though each premise and the conclusion seem reasonable. Believability does not make it valid, and using the word some is not what makes it invalid.

simple.stem: All of the students are tired. Some tired people are irritable. So, some of the students are irritable. Why is this not valid?
options: The irritable tired people need not be any of the students.
The first premise is clearly false about most real students.
The conclusion is too hard to believe.
It contains more than two separate premises.
simple.why: The tired people who are irritable could all be people other than the students, so the conclusion does not follow even though every statement sounds reasonable.

college.stem: A person accepts an invalid argument as logically sound because its conclusion matches what they already think is true. What is this tendency called?
options: Belief bias, judging a syllogism valid when its conclusion is believable.
Status quo bias, sticking with the default when a decision is hard.
The framing effect, letting the wording of a choice shape the decision.
Risk avoidance, steering away from choices with large negative consequences.
college.why: Belief bias is the tendency to think a syllogism is valid if its conclusion is believable; 71% of participants judged invalid, believable conclusions as valid. The other terms describe decision biases, not reasoning about validity.

simple.stem: What is belief bias?
options: Thinking a syllogism is valid because its conclusion is believable.
Thinking a syllogism is invalid because its premises are very long.
Believing that a loss will hurt more than a gain.
Sticking with the default choice when deciding is hard.
simple.why: Belief bias is judging a syllogism valid because its conclusion is believable.

college.stem: A puzzle asks where the cue ball lies in a person’s line of sight, given the positions of a black, green, and red ball on a pool table. How do most people solve it?
options: They imagine how the balls are arranged on the table.
They apply a formal rule for checking whether syllogisms are valid.
They count how many balls sit on each side of the table.
They recall an earlier game that had the same arrangement.
college.why: Most people solve the pool table problem by imagining the arrangement of the balls. That ability to imagine situations is the basis of Johnson-Laird’s mental model proposal.

simple.stem: In the pool table puzzle about the black, green, red, and cue balls, what do most people do to find the answer?
options: They picture the balls on the table in their mind.
They use a formal rule from logic to work it out.
They guess, because the puzzle has no real answer.
They remember a game they once watched on television.
simple.why: Most people imagine how the balls are arranged, which is the idea behind the mental model approach.

college.stem: In Johnson-Laird’s (1999) mental model approach, what is a mental model?
options: A specific situation held in the mind that helps determine whether a syllogism is valid.
A general rule stored in long-term memory that grants permission once a stated condition is met.
A list of premises that all take the form if p, then q.
An emotion that a person predicts feeling about some outcome.
college.why: A mental model is a specific situation held in a person’s mind that can be used to help determine the validity of syllogisms. A rule granting permission is a permission schema.

simple.stem: In Johnson-Laird’s (1999) approach, what is a mental model?
options: A situation pictured in the mind to help judge validity.
A rule that tells you when something is permitted to happen.
A feeling you expect to have about an outcome.
A premise written in the form if p, then q.
simple.why: A mental model is a specific situation held in the mind that helps determine whether a syllogism is valid.

college.stem: Using Johnson-Laird’s (1999) mental model approach, a reasoner finds one arrangement in which the premises are true but the conclusion is false. What follows?
options: It is not valid, since a valid conclusion cannot be refuted by any model of the premises.
The conclusion is valid, since at least one model of the premises can be built.
The conclusion is valid only if the reasoner spotted the exception quickly.
The exception should be ignored, since tentative conclusions are always accepted as they stand.
college.why: A conclusion is valid only if it cannot be refuted by any model of the premises. A single case that refutes it is enough to show that the conclusion does not follow.

simple.stem: Under Johnson-Laird’s (1999) mental model approach, when is a conclusion valid?
options: When no model of the premises can refute it.
When at least one model of the premises fits it.
When the conclusion sounds believable to most people.
When the reasoner reaches it very quickly.
simple.why: A conclusion is valid only if it cannot be refuted by any model of the premises.

college.stem: Which step of Johnson-Laird’s (1999) mental model approach is aimed directly at finding a case that refutes the conclusion?
options: Looking for exceptions that would falsify the model.
Creating an initial model of the situation described.
Generating tentative conclusions about the model.
Rewriting the first premise in the form if p, then q.
college.why: The steps are creating a model, generating tentative conclusions, looking for exceptions to falsify the model, and determining validity. Looking for exceptions is the search for a case that refutes the conclusion.

simple.stem: In Johnson-Laird’s (1999) mental model approach, what is done right after generating tentative conclusions?
options: Look for exceptions that could falsify the model.
Create a model of the situation.
Decide right away that the syllogism must be valid after all.
Add another premise to the syllogism.
simple.why: The order is: create a model, generate tentative conclusions, look for exceptions that falsify the model, then determine validity.

college.stem: Conditional syllogisms have two premises and a conclusion. What form does the first premise take?
options: It takes the form “If p, then q.”
It takes the form “All p are q.”
It takes the form “Some p are not q.”
It takes the form “No p are q.”
college.why: In a conditional syllogism the first premise has the form if p, then q, and there are four major types. Statements with all, some or no belong to categorical syllogisms.

simple.stem: What is the form of the first premise in a conditional syllogism?
options: If p, then q.
All p are q.
Some p are not q.
No p are q.
simple.why: Conditional syllogisms begin with a premise of the form if p, then q.

college.stem: “If I study, I’ll get a good grade. I studied. Therefore, I’ll get a good grade.” Which type of conditional syllogism is this, and how often was it judged correctly?
options: Modus ponens, a valid form that 97% of participants judged correctly.
Modus tollens, a valid form that 60% of participants judged correctly.
An invalid form that only 40% of participants judged correctly.
Modus ponens, an invalid form that 40% of participants judged correctly.
college.why: Syllogism 1, modus ponens, has the second premise p and the conclusion q. It is valid and was judged correctly 97% of the time.

simple.stem: “If I study, I’ll get a good grade. I studied. So, I’ll get a good grade.” Is this valid, and do people judge it well?
options: Yes, and almost everyone judges it correctly.
Yes, but most people judge it incorrectly.
No, and most people notice the error.
No, but most people think it is valid.
simple.why: This is modus ponens, a valid form judged correctly by 97% of participants.

college.stem: “If I study, I’ll get a good grade. I didn’t get a good grade. Therefore, I didn’t study.” How should this conditional syllogism be evaluated?
options: It is valid modus tollens, but only 60% of participants judged it correctly.
It is invalid, and as many as 97% of participants judged it correctly.
It is invalid, because not q can never lead to the conclusion not p.
It is valid modus ponens, which 97% of participants judged correctly.
college.why: Syllogism 2, modus tollens, has the second premise not q and the conclusion not p. It is valid, but only 60% judged it correctly.

simple.stem: “If I study, I’ll get a good grade. I didn’t get a good grade. So, I didn’t study.” Is this valid?
options: Yes, it is valid, though only 60% judge it correctly.
No, it is invalid, though 97% judge it correctly.
No, because a bad grade proves nothing about studying.
Yes, and nearly everyone judges it correctly.
simple.why: This is modus tollens. It is valid, but only 60% of participants judged it correctly.

college.stem: “If I live in Tucson, then I live in Arizona. I live in Arizona. Therefore, I live in Tucson.” What makes this conditional syllogism invalid?
options: Someone can live in Arizona without living in Tucson, so q does not establish p.
Tucson is not in Arizona, so the first premise of the argument is false.
The conclusion is believable, and belief bias is what makes it invalid.
Its second premise is not p, which cannot support any conclusion at all.
college.why: This has the form of syllogism 3, with second premise q and conclusion p. The first premise does not say Tucson is the only place in Arizona, so the conclusion does not follow.

simple.stem: “If I live in Tucson, then I live in Arizona. I live in Arizona. So, I live in Tucson.” Why is this not valid?
options: A person could live somewhere else in Arizona.
Tucson is not actually located in Arizona.
The first premise is written in the wrong order.
A conclusion is never allowed to mention a city.
simple.why: Living in Arizona does not mean living in Tucson, because there are other places in Arizona.

college.stem: “If I study, I’ll get a good grade. I didn’t study. Therefore, I didn’t get a good grade.” How should this conditional syllogism be evaluated?
options: It is not valid, and only 40% of participants judged it correctly.
It is valid, and 97% of participants judged it correctly.
It is valid, because not p always leads to the conclusion not q.
It is not valid, and 60% of participants judged it correctly.
college.why: Syllogism 4 has the second premise not p and the conclusion not q. The first premise says nothing about what happens without studying, so it is not valid, and only 40% judged it correctly.

simple.stem: “If I study, I’ll get a good grade. I didn’t study. So, I didn’t get a good grade.” Is this valid?
options: No, because a good grade might come without studying.
Yes, because not studying always means a bad grade.
Yes, because it has the same form as modus ponens.
No, because the first premise is obviously false.
simple.why: The first premise says only what happens if I study; a good grade could still happen without studying, so the conclusion does not follow.

college.stem: Which pattern holds across the accuracy results for the four types of conditional syllogism?
options: Both valid forms were judged correctly more often than both invalid forms.
Both invalid forms were judged correctly more often than both valid forms.
All four forms were judged correctly about equally often.
Modus tollens was judged correctly more often than modus ponens.
college.why: The valid forms were judged correctly at 97% and 60%, and the invalid forms at 40% each, so both valid forms exceeded both invalid ones. Modus ponens, not modus tollens, was the easiest.

simple.stem: Which conditional syllogism did people judge correctly most often?
options: Modus ponens, judged correctly 97% of the time.
Modus tollens, judged correctly 60% of the time.
Syllogism 3, judged correctly 40% of the time.
Syllogism 4, judged correctly 40% of the time.
simple.why: Modus ponens had the highest accuracy at 97%, followed by modus tollens at 60% and the two invalid forms at 40%.

college.stem: To test the rule “If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other” with cards showing E, K, 4, and 7, which cards must be turned over?
options: E and 7, since only those cards could reveal a violation of the rule.
E and 4, since those cards match the vowel and the even number.
Only the E, since the rule begins by mentioning a vowel.
All four cards, since any one of them could hide a vowel.
college.why: E must be turned over, and so must the 7, because a vowel behind it would break the rule. A 4 cannot break the rule, yet 46% chose it and only 7% chose the 7.

simple.stem: In the Wason four-card problem, the cards show E, K, 4, and 7, and the rule is “if vowel, then even number.” Which two cards must be turned over?
options: The E card and the 7 card.
The E card and the 4 card.
The K card and the 4 card.
The K card and the 7 card.
simple.why: Only E and 7 could show the rule is broken. Many people wrongly pick the 4, which cannot break the rule.

college.stem: A scientist tests the claim that every swan is white by searching specifically for a swan that is not white. Which principle is she following?
options: The falsification principle, seeking cases that could show the rule is false.
A confirmation strategy, seeking cases that show the rule holds true.
Belief bias, accepting the rule because its conclusion is believable.
The status quo bias, leaving the rule untested because the choice is hard.
college.why: The falsification principle says that to test a rule, you must look for situations that falsify it. Most participants fail to do this in the abstract four-card problem.

simple.stem: What does the falsification principle say?
options: To test a rule, look for cases that could prove it false.
To test a rule, look only for the cases that agree with it.
A rule is correct if it sounds believable.
A rule is true if most people accept it.
simple.why: To test a rule, you must look for situations that could falsify it, not cases that confirm it.

college.stem: When the Wason four-card problem was restated as “If drinking beer, then 21 years old,” how did performance change compared with the vowel-and-number version?
options: Correct responses greatly increased once the rule was put in concrete everyday terms.
Correct responses dropped, because the drinking rule was harder to follow.
Correct responses stayed at the same level as in the abstract version.
Participants declined to answer, because the drinking rule felt unfamiliar and confusing to them.
college.why: When the problem is stated in concrete everyday terms, correct responses greatly increase. People are familiar with rules like the drinking-age rule, so the improvement is the opposite of a drop.

simple.stem: What happens when the Wason four-card problem uses an everyday rule about drinking age?
options: Many more people answer it correctly.
Far fewer people answer it correctly.
The same number of people answer correctly.
People refuse to answer the problem at all.
simple.why: Stating the problem in concrete everyday terms greatly increases correct responses.

college.stem: The rule “If you are 21 or older, you may drink beer” matches which kind of structure that helps people with the concrete four-card problems?
options: A permission schema, in which satisfying condition A allows action B.
A reversed conditional, in which carrying out B proves that A was satisfied.
Belief bias, in which a believable conclusion makes an argument valid.
Risk aversion, in which a loss is expected to weigh more than a gain.
college.why: A permission schema states that if A is satisfied, B can be carried out. Such schemas are used in the concrete versions because people are familiar with these rules.

simple.stem: What is a permission schema?
options: A rule that if A is satisfied, B can be done.
A rule that if B is done, A must be true.
A rule that believable conclusions are valid.
A rule that losses matter more than gains.
simple.why: A permission schema says that if A is satisfied, B can be carried out.

college.stem: Which conclusion about the concrete four-card problems fits both the point that context is important and the point that familiarity is not always important?
options: A setting that calls up a permission schema helps, but familiarity alone does not explain it.
Familiarity alone explains every improvement observed, so the context of the rule does not matter at all.
Context matters only for abstract letters and numbers, not for everyday rules.
Neither context nor familiarity has any measurable effect on performance.
college.why: Context is important, because the same logic becomes easier in a setting that calls up a permission schema. Familiarity is not always important, so it cannot account for the improvement on its own.

simple.stem: What two conclusions follow from the concrete versions of the four-card problem?
options: Context is important, but familiarity is not always important.
Familiarity is always important, but context does not matter.
Neither context nor familiarity affects performance.
Context matters only for letters and numbers.
simple.why: Context is important, and familiarity is not always important.
